transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Chen (Redwood AE), Alice Park (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SRE) -- Priya Nair (Horizon CTO), Samir Patel (Infra), Lena Ortiz (ML Platform), Omar Khan (Security)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be noisy):
- Focus on p99/p95 tail; Horizon needs <200ms p95 for short prompts and <350ms p99 for 8k token scoring pipelines.
- Discussed streaming tradeoffs, kv cache hit rates, batching windows and timeouts, and quantization impacts on latency and quality.
- Agreed to run synthetic benchmarks and a small private POC.

00:00:05 Marcus: okay thanks everyone for joining, we'll keep this focused on tail latency stuff that you asked for priya, so agenda is p95/p99 numbers, streaming vs non-streaming, kv cache behaviour, batching and quantization, and then open items.
00:00:18 Priya: yeah thanks marcus, our biggest problem is spikes - usually p95 is okay-ish but p99 blows up and our users notice, especially during short chat things, the real time assistant latency is the UX blocker.
00:00:35 Alice: can you give us ballparks for your current numbers and env? like cloud provider, single region, whether you use a proxy or in-region vpc peering?
00:00:48 Samir: sure, we're on GCP europe-west1, fronted by our edge proxy in the same region. typical baseline for a simple 512 token response is p50 ~ 70ms, p95 ~ 220ms, p99 ~ 800ms under peak. we also have a 2-hop internal proxy for request routing which adds ~20-40ms occasionally.
00:01:10 Diego: that two-hop thing is important, we've seen network hops dominate tails when the model servers are fast.
00:01:22 Marcus: right, the breakdown matters: client->edge, edge->intra-proxy, proxy->inference. are you doing streaming to the client?
00:01:31 Lena: yes streaming for chat, but for some of our scoring pipelines we also need non-streaming full responses for downstream postprocessing.
00:01:43 Alice: okay, so two different patterns: low-latency streaming where you want first-token p95 small, and batchy non-streaming scoring where p99 matters across full sequence. we'll talk about both.
00:01:58 00:02:05 Marcus: quick note, when we talk about p99 numbers, we're measuring server-side service time (inference only) vs end-to-end. we should clarify what horizon wants to use as an SLO.
00:02:14 Priya: end-to-end is what our product cares about, but if we can get server-side numbers we can budget network and proxy. we want under 200ms p95 end-to-end for typical chat.
00:02:27 Alice: got it. some common sources of tail: preemption on shared nodes, cold kv cache (prefix cache misses), sudden long sequences that trigger switching kernels, and micro-GC or disk IO on host.
00:02:45 Samir: preemption yeah, we're worried about shared hosted modes. dedicated solves a lot of that but costs more. we need guidance on dedicated vs hosted for predictable tails.
00:02:58 Marcus: dedicated helps a lot; for p99 stability we recommend reserved pools and pinning to specific instance types. also fast network (single region, colocated) to avoid cross-zone jumps.
00:03:12 00:03:30 Alice: about KV cache: we do two-layer caching - prefix-level cache and per-session kv for decoding. Misses can add 50-200ms depending on if we need to reconstruct state or fall back to full attention. do you prewarm sessions?
00:03:46 Lena: no automated prewarm today, we rely on traffic to warm up but that causes the spikes.
00:03:55 Diego: prewarm + keepalive threads are super effective: keep the KV cache hot for frequent session ids and rehydrate from snapshot for longer-lived users. rehydration cost depends on NVMe vs in-memory.
00:04:08 Priya: curious about quantization — we see quality drift when moving from fp16 to int8 for some of our prompts. does Redwood support mixed quantization?
00:04:19 Alice: yes we support mixed precision paths and per-layer quantization profiles. int8 can reduce single-token latency by ~10-25% on GPU inference, but it can also increase variability if the kernels use fallback paths for certain ops. we recommend testing with your eval set.
00:04:36 00:04:50 Marcus: also important is kernel selection and sequence-length tuned kernels. if you suddenly get a 4k token request on a 512-optimized pipeline, the runtime switches kernels which can add 100-300ms tail. do you have long-tail sequence length distribution?
00:05:05 Samir: our median is ~160 tokens but we have bursts that go to 2k for context windows. those bursts align with p99 spikes.
00:05:14 Alice: you can mitigate with routing by sequence length: route long sequences to a variant optimized for long contexts and keep short-context pools for chat. that reduces p99 for the chat traffic.
00:05:27 Omar: on the security side, we're concerned about VPC/on-prem and network egress - will dedicated/private increase our attack surface or change audit log behavior?
00:05:38 Diego: private deployments are basically on your VPC with customer-controlled networking and KMS integrations; audit logs are shipped to your logging buckets and we can provide syslog / SIEM integration. latency is mostly about the peering path and MTU/keepalive.
00:05:52 00:06:05 Marcus: a note on streaming vs non-streaming: streaming typically reduces perceived latency because you send partial tokens as soon as they're available; first-token latency is the key metric. non-streaming needs full decode which amplifies p99 because anything blocking at the tail delays whole payload.
00:06:21 Lena: does streaming increase server CPU due to more churn? we worry about throughput hit when supporting many streaming connections.
00:06:31 Alice: it does increase connection churn but techniques like multiplexed connections, HTTP/2 or gRPC streams, and batching at the token level help. Redwood's runtime supports multiplexed streaming so we avoid per-token round trip heavy overhead.
00:06:45 Priya: about measuring p99 — what do you recommend instrumenting so we can separate network vs server latency?
00:06:54 Marcus: instrument client-side timestamps, edge proxy logs, and server-side decode timing. correlate traces via request IDs; we provide tracing hooks and token-level breakdowns in the console. that way you can split p99 into network, queuing, and inference.
00:07:10 Samir: small aside: our internal proxy occasionally does buffer bloat at 2x concurrent throughput; would that show up as increased queuing times?
00:07:18 Diego: yes, buffer bloat looks like increased queuing before the server. setting lower queue depth, TCP keepalive tuning, and using HTTP/2 flow control alleviates it. we'll share recommended tcp/tls settings.
00:07:32 00:07:50 Alice: let's walk through a hypothetical measurement: if server-side inference p99 is 280ms but you have two network hops adding 30-40ms each and 30ms edge processing, your end-to-end p99 becomes ~380-430ms. so small network hops matter a lot.
00:08:06 Priya: that matches what we see. often our p99 is 700-800ms but when we subtract egress and proxy we still have a 300-350ms server tail.
00:08:18 Marcus: mitigation patterns: 1) pin critical routes to dedicated pools; 2) prewarm and keep KV hot; 3) separate short-context and long-context pools; 4) apply request prioritization during overload; 5) enable adaptive batching with strict max-latency windows; 6) consider mixed quantization but validate quality.
00:08:36 Lena: can you explain adaptive batching and strict max-latency windows? our current batching groups by 20ms window which sometimes increases first-token latency.
00:08:47 Alice: adaptive batching grows batch size up to a max while ensuring a max-wait threshold; e.g., you can set max-wait=8ms for first-token-sensitive chat and max-batch=32 for throughput. the runtime will flush when either threshold hits. it's a balance: smaller windows reduce p95 but lower GPU utilization. we provide cost estimates for different policies.
00:09:08 00:09:25 Diego: and don't forget continuous batching — we keep multiple in-flight batches on GPUs to improve throughput while controlling tail latencies via priority slots.
00:09:36 Samir: about kernel fallbacks you mentioned earlier — are those deterministic? we get a lot of variance when falling back to generic kernels.
00:09:44 Alice: fallbacks happen when quantized kernels can't handle certain ops; they're deterministic given input shapes but unpredictable in production unless you condition models or apply conservative quantization. our compiler flags kernels during model onboarding and we can provide a regression report showing which layers cause fallbacks.
00:10:02 00:10:20 Marcus: let's talk concrete POC. we'll run two experiments: 1) hosted dedicated pool with streaming enabled, short-context routing, and prewarm; 2) a private VPC deployment where we can measure network hop impact. we'll run identical synthetic load and your real prompt set.
00:10:36 Priya: timeline?
00:10:38 Marcus: if you provide prompt set by Thursday we'll run synthetic tests by next Monday and share a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and breakdowns. then week after we can spin a private POC cluster for a deeper run.
00:10:51 00:11:05 Alice: measurable items in the spreadsheet will include: request timestamps, first-token latency, full-response latency, KV hit/miss, batch size, kernel type, quantization profile, and network hop latencies.
00:11:18 Omar: on the security docs — we need SOC2, SAML SSO integration notes, and KMS flow diagrams. are those ready?
00:11:26 Marcus: yes we'll send SOC2 + ISO docs and an architecture guide for private deployments; for SAML we have a quickstart and can do a short integration call.
00:11:36 Samir: cost question: dedicated vs hosted — if we pin short-context pools what uplift in cost should we expect?
00:11:44 Marcus: rough rule: dedicated pools for predictable low p99 increase costs by 30-80% depending on utilization and instance type; but when you factor in user retention and SLA benefits it often pays off. our Optimize toolkit can give you model/quantization suggestions to lower token cost while preserving latency.
00:11:59 00:12:15 Priya: any quick wins we can try immediately?
00:12:18 Alice: three quick wins: 1) reduce proxy buffering and tune keepalive; 2) split short vs long context routing; 3) enable KV prewarm for active sessions. these should drop p99 significantly without big infra changes.
00:12:33 Lena: about prewarm — how do we manage memory if we keep many session KV in memory? concern about OOM or eviction thrashing.
00:12:42 Diego: we use LRU with size caps and snapshotting to NVMe; for very active users keep hot in-memory, others rehydrate lazily. you can set per-customer caps. we'll share recommended defaults.
00:12:56 00:13:10 Marcus: any other questions on quantization or batching tradeoffs?
00:13:13 Samir: curious if you have hard numbers on int8 p99 behavior vs fp16 for same model.
00:13:19 Alice: from internal runs on a typical LLaMA-type 13B variant, fp16 p99 single-token was ~120ms, int8 ~95ms but with occasional 1.2-1.5x outliers when kernel fallbacks triggered for specific ops. for critical flows we recommend mixed precision or per-layer quantization audit. we'll include these numbers in the bench sheet.
00:13:43 00:13:58 Priya: let's clarify metrics: we want server-side p95 < 150ms and end-to-end p95 < 200ms. p99 target end-to-end < 350ms. are those achievable?
00:14:06 Marcus: achievable with dedicated short-context pools, prewarm, and routing; private VPC network tuning will help. we can't promise until we run your prompt set, but topologies we propose routinely hit those targets for similar customers.
00:14:24 Lena: what's the effect of TLS termination on the edge vs instance-level TLS? we run mTLS inside cluster and TLS at edge, does that add latency?
00:14:33 Diego: TLS termination at edge is standard; if you do TLS inside the cluster you'll add CPU overhead but negligible network latency. keep TLS session reuse and HTTP/2 to reduce handshake costs.
00:14:45 00:14:58 Marcus: last piece: priority routing during overload. we can reserve slots for interactive chat and degrade scoring jobs when overloaded, reducing p99 for interactive users.
00:15:06 Priya: that sounds useful; we'd need API-level priority markings and RBAC for who can call those routes.
00:15:13 Marcus: we support per-route priority and RBAC in Console; we'll demo in the follow-up.
00:15:22 00:15:35 Alice: okay recap of action items: we'll run synthetics, send security docs, and schedule the on-prem design workshop. any other asks from horizon?
00:15:44 Priya: please include a comparison versus managed offerings like OpenAI/Anthropic for p99 behavior and costs in the spreadsheet.
00:15:53 Marcus: we can provide a rough comparative column; will annotate assumptions.
00:16:00 00:16:20 Diego: i'll follow up with network tuning doc and keepalive settings.
00:16:27 Marcus: great. thanks everybody. we'll follow up with the bench sheet and schedule next workshop.
